n: At Lystra Paul met Timothy, a young disciple with a believing Jewish mother and a Greek father. Timothy would become one of Paul’s closest companions.

f.g: Timothy — Greek for “honoring God.” Two New Testament letters are addressed to him.

n: The believers in Lystra and Iconium spoke highly of Timothy. His good reputation prepared him for a calling.
Paul had Timothy circumcised — not for salvation, but so Jewish audiences would accept him, since his mother was Jewish. Paul was flexible on customs when the gospel’s core wasn’t at stake.

f.w: circumcised him because of the Jews

n: As they traveled, they shared the Jerusalem council’s decisions with each branch so they could follow them.
The branches grew stronger in faith and larger in number every day.
The Holy Ghost prevented them from preaching in the province of Asia (western Turkey) at that time. Sometimes the Spirit guides by closing doors.

f.g: The Roman province of Asia in western Asia Minor, with Ephesus as its chief city — not the continent.

n: They tried to go north into Bithynia, but again the Spirit would not allow it. They didn’t yet know where God wanted them.

f.g: Tried, attempted.
Did not allow them.

n: Passing through Mysia, they arrived at Troas, a port on the Aegean Sea near ancient Troy.

f.g: Alexandria Troas, a seaport in northwest Asia Minor.

n: In a night vision, Paul saw a man from Macedonia pleading, “Come over and help us.” This call brought the gospel into Europe for the first time.

f.g: The Roman province of northern Greece.

f.w: Come over into Macedonia, and help us

n: Notice the shift to “we” — Luke, the author, apparently joins Paul here. The group concluded God was calling them and left immediately.

f.g: The first of the “we” passages in Acts, suggesting Luke was present as an eyewitness.
Concluding with confidence.

n: With favorable winds they sailed quickly to the island of Samothrace and then to Neapolis, the port for Philippi.

f.g: “New city” — modern Kavala, Greece.

n: Philippi was a leading city and a Roman colony — a little Rome, full of retired soldiers and proud of Roman citizenship. That detail matters later in the chapter.

f.g: A city with special Roman legal status, governed as an extension of Rome.

n: With apparently no synagogue in town, they found a group of women praying by the river on the Sabbath, sat down, and taught them.

f.g: Was customarily held.
Gathered, came regularly.

n: Lydia, a businesswoman who sold expensive purple cloth, was a Gentile worshipper of God. The Lord opened her heart to Paul’s message.

f.g: Purple dye was costly; dealers in purple cloth were often prosperous.
A city in western Asia Minor famous for its dyeing industry.

n: Lydia and her household were baptized — Paul’s first converts in Europe. She warmly insisted the missionaries stay in her home.

f.g: Urged strongly, insisted.

n: A slave girl with a spirit of fortune-telling met them. Her owners made a lot of money from her predictions.

f.g: Greek “a python spirit” — linked to the oracle of Apollo at Delphi.
Fortune-telling.

n: She followed them, shouting that they were servants of the Most High God. Her words were true, but coming from an evil spirit they could confuse or discredit the message.
After many days, Paul, troubled, commanded the spirit in Jesus Christ’s name to leave her, and it left immediately. Priesthood authority in Christ’s name has power over evil.

f.w: in the name of Jesus Christ

n: Her owners, seeing their income gone, seized Paul and Silas and dragged them before the city authorities. Greed, not religion, drove the attack.

f.w: the hope of their gains was gone

n: They accused the missionaries of disturbing the peace, playing on local prejudice by stressing that they were Jews.

f.g: The two chief officials governing a Roman colony.

n: They charged them with promoting customs illegal for Romans. Roman law frowned on spreading new foreign religions among citizens.
A mob formed. The officials had Paul and Silas stripped and beaten with rods, without a trial.
After a severe beating, they were thrown into prison, and the jailer was ordered to guard them closely.

f.g: Lashes or blows from a beating.

n: The jailer put them in the innermost cell and locked their feet in stocks — wooden blocks that held the legs painfully apart.

f.g: A wooden frame clamping the feet, often stretched to cause pain.

n: Beaten and chained, at midnight Paul and Silas prayed and sang hymns to God — and the other prisoners listened. Their praise in suffering was itself a sermon.
Suddenly a great earthquake shook the prison. The doors flew open and everyone’s chains came loose.
The jailer woke, saw the doors open, and drew his sword to kill himself, assuming the prisoners had escaped. Under Roman practice he would face harsh punishment.
Paul shouted to stop him: “Don’t hurt yourself — we’re all here!” Paul cared for the very man who had locked him in.
The jailer called for a light, rushed in, and fell trembling at their feet.
He brought them out and asked the most important question anyone can ask: “What must I do to be saved?”

f.w: what must I do to be saved?

n: Their answer: believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and you and your household will be saved. Faith in Christ is the starting point, leading to repentance, baptism, and a new life.

f.w: Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ

n: They taught the gospel to the jailer and his whole household. Belief needs teaching to give it content.
That very night the jailer washed their wounds, and then he and his family were baptized. The washings came full circle: he cleansed their wounds, and baptism cleansed him.

f.w: was baptized, he and all his

n: He brought them home, fed them, and rejoiced with his whole family in their new faith in God.

f.g: Food in general.

n: In the morning, the magistrates sent officers with orders to release them — perhaps thinking a beating and a night in jail had been enough.

f.g: Lictors — officers who attended the magistrates and carried rods.

n: The jailer happily passed on the news and told them they could leave in peace.

Paul refused to slip away quietly. As Roman citizens, they had been illegally beaten without trial. He demanded the officials come and escort them out publicly — likely to protect the new believers’ reputation.

f.g: Roman citizens were legally protected from being beaten without trial.
Secretly, quietly.

n: The magistrates were alarmed to learn they had abused Roman citizens — a serious crime that could cost them their positions.
The officials came, apologized, escorted them out, and politely asked them to leave the city.

f.g: Begged, pleaded with.

n: Before leaving, they visited Lydia’s house to encourage the believers. The persecuted missionaries comforted those they were leaving behind.
